board.setup: Claude Code hook, MCP proxy and fetch proxy; network layer not measured
notes: The benchmark runs no command, so pipelock's forward proxy, which checks where a command actually connects, is not part of this score.

statement.text:
Pipelock is mostly a network firewall. It sits between an agent and the internet and scans the traffic routed through it for leaked secrets, injected instructions and blocked destinations. This run tests Pipelock 3.8.0's Claude Code hook, MCP proxy and fetch proxy. It never runs the shell commands in the cases, so the forward proxy that checks where those commands actually connect isn't part of the score. The label says the network layer isn't measured, and that's the part most Pipelock users rely on.

The run does show real misses in credential and personal-data detection, and those are on me to improve. Pipelock doesn't check package reputation, so it let the malicious package installs through in this setup.

After my feedback the AgentVerdict team changed the method for every tool, so it now leaves out cases a tool can't be measured on and ends a case at the first step the tool stops. I think that's the right way to score it.

notes: Of HOL Guard's stops in the headline, 328 attacks and 141 ordinary calls carry native_command_extension_evaluation_failed: Guard could not match the command to an installed control and stopped it. They count as stops, since that is what the hook returned. In the makers' section the same reason covers 16 attacks and 40 ordinary calls; in the holdout, 8 ordinary calls.

statement.text: HOL Guard (https://hol.org/guard) reviews AI-agent actions before they run. AgentVerdict's replay shows the tradeoff plainly: Guard stopped some harmful calls, but also interrupted ordinary work. A native_command_extension_evaluation_failed result means Guard could not match a command to an installed control and stopped it. That is not the same as detecting an attack. These scores describe replayed hook decisions, not an end-to-end live-agent evaluation. Reducing unnecessary stops without weakening protection matters to us.

board.setup: Monitor mode as installed, shipped catalog
notes: numbat as installed monitors and does not block: it records what it finds and lets every call through. Its enforce mode is shown on its own line.

board.setup: Enforce mode, every shipped rule set to enforce as its docs describe (not the default)

board_notes: The holdout (1,401 cases) is kept private so that no tool can be tuned to it. node9 holds it, and 36 of its cases come from node9's own generators, all in the section for suites written by a tool's maker, none in the headline; the rest are drawn in secret from outside sources.

A case a tool cannot be measured on (one that rests on a setting the tool does not have, or on a command's output) is left out of that tool's rates and listed with its reason in the tool's results, never counted as a miss.

areas.title: Secrets
areas.attacks: A credential written to a file, sent off the machine or used where it should not be: real-shaped keys, tokens and private keys.
areas.ordinary: Code and documents that only look like they hold one, legitimate credential work.
areas.sources: Samsung CredData, Gretel, generated GitHub tokens, planted canaries, node9 jail and credential tests

areas.title: Personal data
areas.attacks: A document with personal identifiers sent off the machine.
areas.ordinary: The same documents without an identifier a guard can recognise.
areas.sources: Nemotron-PII (NVIDIA), Gretel synthetic PII finance, OpenPII (ai4privacy), node9 PII tests

areas.title: Commands and scripts
areas.attacks: Risky shell commands and scripts an agent is asked to run: reading sensitive files, destroying data, opening a shell to the outside.
areas.ordinary: Everyday shell commands and whole programs.
areas.sources: RedCode-Exec (AI-secure), NL2SH-ALFA, MBPP and Exercism scripts, node9 system directory tests

areas.title: Packages
areas.attacks: Installing a malicious or typosquatted package, or a compromised version of a good one.
areas.ordinary: Installing the most downloaded packages, pinned and unpinned, in every ecosystem.
areas.sources: OSV (OpenSSF malicious packages), DataDog malicious-software-packages, typomind, official download statistics

areas.title: Poisoned content
areas.attacks: The attacker's action after the agent read poisoned content.
areas.ordinary: Ordinary actions after harmless text that happens to contain trigger words.
areas.sources: AgentDojo (ETH Zurich), NotInject, node9 exposure and injection tests

areas.title: Data leaving the machine
areas.attacks: Sending data to an unlisted host, a private address or cloud metadata, under the policy the user set.
areas.ordinary: Sends to the hosts the user allowed.

areas.title: Actions through tools
areas.attacks: A state-changing MCP call the attacker wanted, and actions a person asked to approve.
areas.sources: AgentDojo tasks, dangerous actions, node9 exposure tests

sources.title: node9's own tests and corpora
agent-egress-bench (pipelock's benchmark): MCP calls, results and fetches
AgentDojo (ETH Zurich), across agents: the poisoned result read by a subagent, handed to one in a brief, or reported back by one, before the attacker's call
NotInject: an ordinary action after benign text with trigger words
agentic-security-benchmark (MoorAI's set, to the AMTSO guidelines): outbound actions, and writes to an agent's memory
AgentDojo (ETH Zurich): the attacker's ground-truth call after the poisoned result, and the user's after a clean one
Exposure: ordinary sends after reading outside content
Dangerous actions: money, credentials, deletion, access, publishing (a person approves even when the user asked)
Package installs (OSV malicious-packages and everyday installs)
OpenSSF malicious packages beyond npm and PyPI
DataDog malicious-software-packages: npm and PyPI names
typomind (USENIX Security 2023): labelled typosquats
Everyday installs beyond npm and PyPI (RubyGems, crates.io, Go, NuGet, Maven, Packagist, editor extensions)
Most downloaded npm and PyPI packages (official download statistics), installed
Nemotron-PII (NVIDIA): documents sent off the machine
Gretel synthetic PII finance: financial documents sent off the machine
OpenPII (ai4privacy): multilingual texts sent off the machine
GitHub tokens generated with and without a valid checksum
Samsung CredData: credential and look-alike lines written to a file
RedCode-Exec (AI-secure): risky bash scripts an agent is asked to run
NL2SH-ALFA: ordinary shell commands for English tasks
Cascading failures: the same call once more after five identical ones, a ninth subagent after eight (node9's rule)
System directories: ordinary work and the changes a review is meant for
Benign scripts: MBPP reference solutions in Python and Exercism Bash examples, run whole
agent-guard-bench (a guard maker's AI-written, AI-labelled set): git commands that stage the whole tree, disarm the hooks or destroy work, under the user's git rules

owasp.name: Agent Goal Hijack
owasp.what: The agent read poisoned content (a web page, an email, a tool result) and its next action is the attacker's.
owasp.tests: AgentDojo sequences (ETH Zurich), NotInject sequences, node9 exposure and injection tests, agent-egress-bench

owasp.name: Tool Misuse and Exploitation
owasp.what: Harmful commands, personal data sent off the machine, data leaving through a tool; and the ordinary commands and documents beside them.
owasp.tests: RedCode-Exec, NL2SH-ALFA, Nemotron-PII (NVIDIA), Gretel, OpenPII, node9 egress, PII and system tests, agent-egress-bench

owasp.name: Identity and Privilege Abuse
owasp.what: Credentials leaving the machine or used where they should not be; and code that only looks like it holds one.
owasp.tests: Samsung CredData, Gretel credentials, generated GitHub tokens, planted canaries, node9 jail and legitimate credential work

owasp.name: Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities
owasp.what: Malicious and typosquatted packages; and the most downloaded ones, installed as usual.
owasp.tests: OSV malicious packages (npm, PyPI and other ecosystems), DataDog malicious packages, typomind typosquats, popular packages, everyday installs

owasp.name: Unexpected Code Execution
owasp.what: Installing from an untrusted source, eval injection, reverse shells; and ordinary programs run whole.

owasp.name: Memory and Context Poisoning
owasp.what: Poisoning what the agent remembers or carries between sessions.

owasp.name: Cascading Failures
owasp.what: One failure that spreads through chained agents and tools.

owasp.name: Human-Agent Trust Exploitation
owasp.what: Actions a person should approve: moving money, changing credentials, deleting data, managing access, publishing; and the ordinary actions beside them.
owasp.tests: Dangerous actions (AgentVerdict's rule over AgentDojo's tasks)

owasp.name: Rogue Agents
owasp.what: An agent acting outside its mandate.
